 What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case? 
 
PE 651.385 7 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
This policy briefing explores possible policy lessons from the downfall of Wirecard, the German fintech 
payment provider, then listed in the country’s top stock market segment DAX. In our view, all five lines 
of defence against corporate fraud and deception have failed in one way or another: the company’s 
internal control system, its supervisory board, its external audit, the oversight bodies for financial 
reporting and auditing and, last but not least, the market supervisor BaFin. The slow unravell ing of 
Wirecard is surprising as there were a number of signals suggesting fraudulent behaviour years before 
its eventual revelation. Our analysis finds a root cause to be a flawed market and institutional oversi ght 
architecture, implicating all five lines of defence. In its current form, it is not sufficiently fit to preserve 
market integrity and investor protection. To improve the system, we suggest changes at the national 
as well as the European level. In fact, we understand the Wirecard scandal in German y  a s  a  po t en t ially  
pivotal event for Europe’s capital market, triggering a regulatory reform of financial market oversight 
that ultimately improves its competitiveness among global capital markets.  
Our policy conclusions aim to ensure the integrity of th e capital market by strengtheni ng 
accountability. Towards this end, we propose to improve the information flow to markets and 
supervision, respecting whistleblowing and short selling as important information sources. The 
accountability of external auditors  has to be strengthened so that they have stronger incentives to 
detect accounting manipulations and fraud, which enhances the information value of audits for capi tal 
markets and ultimately the accuracy and credibility of firms’ financial reporting. To strengthen internal 
control mechanisms, listed firms should be legally required to have an appropriate and effective 
internal control system. We recommend that its head reports to the supervisory board, not to the 
management board. Internal control audits should be considered. BaFin needs considerably stronger 
supervisory and enforcement powers in order to live up to its overarching mandate as to market 
integrity and investor protection. We recommend entrusting the agency with broad enforcement 
powers, including forensic and investigative tools. These changes also entail relegating self-regulatory 
enforcement bodies such as FREP in Germany to a purely ancillary, optional function. Along with 
strengthening its powers, we propose to clearly establish the supervis ory agency’s accountability for 
fulfilling its overarching  mandate. This accountability requires an appropriate level of institutional 
independence as well as sufficient resources to fulfil its tasks. Finally, we submit that Wirecard holds 
lessons that go well beyond the German market and oversight system. Considering the negative 
spillovers of fraud cases in a European market and anticipating that national interests may play a rol e 
in market supervision, which also creates unhelpful externalities, we suggest establishing a European 
Single Capital Market Supervisory body (ESCMS). Given that national supervisors are highly 
knowledgeable of the local situation, we recommend integrating them into a European supervisory 
network. A hub -and-spoke architecture with  clear reporting lines to the hub will also introduce an 
element of institutional independence into national agencies and make regulatory capture harder.

PREFACE 
Wirecard was initially founded as a German fintech in Munich in 1999. After an interlude o f insolvency in 
2001, Wirecard was listed in 2005 in the Deutsche Börse’s Prime Standard market segment. It became a 
leading fintech company in Germany, focusing on payment and risk management services in the debit and 
credit card business in Europe, Asia and America. It moved up to the Tec Dax in 2006 and, in 2018, to the 
DAX, the top index segment of the German market. Starting in 2015, there were allegations about 
accounting inconsistencies, esp. in the Financial Times (FT) which wrote about a “House of Wirecards”, partly  
based on whistleblower information about the Singapore operations of the firm. In 2016, an analyst report,  
known as the Zatarra Report, accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud. Following this report, there 
was significant short selling of the Wirecard stock, some of which BaFin referred to the German prosecutor 
for market abuse, leading to indictments and settlements. 
After another detailed report in the FT, in January 2019, BaFin requested an investigation of Wirecard’s 
financial statements by the Financial Reporting Enf orcement Panel (FREP). FREP is a private agency,  
entrusted with a public mandate. It has been set up as the “first step” in the German “two-step procedure” of 
financial reporting enforcement. When short selling peaked again, BaFin intervened and prohibited  
increases in net short sale positions for a period of two months, in accordance with the European Securities 
and Markets Authority (ESMA). It also filed a criminal complaint against a number of short sellers as well as 
the journalist who had authored the January FT article. The FT continued to report on allegedly inflated sales 
and profit numbers at Wirecard, backed up with internal documents. In October 2019, KPMG was hired by 
Wirecard to conduct a forensic investigation. The report was published with sev eral delays in April 2020, 
stating that KPMG was unable to verify the existence of 1 billion Euros in foreign bank accounts. BaFin filed 
a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020 and, a few days later, the company filed for bankruptc y 
acknowledging that financial assets of 1.9 billion Euros were missing.2

Christian Leuz and Loriana Pelizzon. We are grateful for discussions with, and valuable comments from

1. MARKETS, OVERSIGHT AND THE WIRECARD CASE 
Capital markets are a powerful instrument to allocate resources from investors to issuers, i.e. firms and 
states. A well-functioning capital market is a key determinant of economic growth as well as of private 
and public wealth. The term “cap ital market” refers to a complex institutional structure, compri si ng 
various contractual arrangements, regulatory or legal rules, and enforcement mechanisms, physical 
and virtual trading venues, and a variety of financial instruments, like stocks, bonds, d erivatives, and 
currencies, owned by a variety of investors. Together with the banking system, the capital market 
provides the financial infrastructure of the economy. As in banking, trust in the proper functioning of 
the capital market is a prerequisite f or it to play its beneficial role. It is, for instance, critical for broad 
investor participation (Guiso et al. 2008). 
Scandals such as Wirecard can destroy investor trust in capital markets working fairly and with integri ty, 
which in turn creates negative spillover effects. Scandals can make it harder for other, non-fraudulent 
firms to raise capital as investors raise the risk premium or choose to no longer participate in the market 
(e.g. Aggarwal and Wu 2006; Kyle and Viswanathan 2008; Giannetti and Wang 2016; Gurun et al. 2018). 
It is for this reason that fraud deserves attention. In essence, trust in the capital market is a (valuable) 
public good. Among other things, it requires assurance that corporate insiders do not embezzle 
investors’ money (e.g. Shleifer and Wolfenzon 2002). 
For this reason, countries’ legal frameworks and capital market regulation aim to facilitate capital 
formation and market transactions and, at the same time, to protect market integrity and investors. 
This typically encompasses f inancial reporting and disclosure requirements, anti- fraud provisi ons, 
restrictions on insider trading and market manipulation, limits on self -dealing by corporate insiders, 
and corporate governance stipulations. However, rules alone are not sufficient. Investors need to trust 
that compliance with these rules is monitored and, if necessary, enforced. Therefore, well-functioning 
capital markets also require effective public and private enforcement mechanisms. Effective capital 
market regulation and enforcement contribute to the development of the capital market (e.g. La P orta 
et al. 2006) and lower firms’ cost of capital (Hail and Leuz 2006; 2009). These arguments form the 
economic basis for supervisory mandates in many countries. To illustrate: the US Securities and 
Exchange Commission (SEC) describes its mission as one “to protect investors, maintain fair, orderly, 
and efficient markets, and facilitate capital formation” (SEC 2013). In a similar spirit, BaFin’s webs ite  
states: “The objective of securities supervision is to ensure the transparency and integrity of the 
financial market and the protection of investors.” 
Consistent with these objectives and the above economic arguments, we use market integrity and 
investor protection as the guiding principles for the analysis in this policy briefing. The goal is to draw 
a number of wider lessons from the Wirecard case. At the start, it is natural to ask: Why did the scandal 
– fraud and deception at Wirecard – remain undetected for so long? Who or what is to blame? Was it 
due to deficiencies in institutional and legal design, supervisory failures, professional negligence or 
(moral) failures of th e perpetrators?3 Common sense dictates that, in the end, the scandal is due to a 
mix of reasons. In this briefing we will try to identify major reasons for the occurrence and slow 
detection of the scandal, emphasi sing the role of institutional deficiencies. These deficiencies can, in 
principle, be mitigated by reforming market and oversight institutions as well as supervisory agencies.4

We realise that, even with much more stringent market and institutional oversight, fraud will probabl y 
never be completely prevented. But this cannot and should not be the overall objective of regulatory 
effort anyway, as it would be excessively costly to businesses, and stifle capital formation and marke t 
transactions. That said, well-functioning capital markets needs equally well- functioning market and 
regulatory oversight. Without it, capital markets cannot deliver their positive contributions to the 
formation and allocation of capital in an economy. The Wirecard scandal has revealed maj or 
weaknesses in this ove rsight in Germany, especially with respect to investor protection and market 
integrity. Moreover, we believe the Wirecard scandal holds broader lessons for European capital market 
oversight.  
In this policy briefing, we discuss four shortcomings of market a nd institutional oversight that the 
Wirecard case has brought to light: Shortcomings with respect to whistleblowers a nd in fo rm at io n flows  
into prices (section 2.1); Weaknesses of external audits, internal controls but also market forces when it 
comes to Wirecard’s accounting information (section 2.2); Limitations in the supervisor’s investigation 
and enforcement powers, limiting its ability to take the appropriate action when needed (sections 2.3 
and 2.4); The potential for negative externalities and the ri sk of supervisory capture in a fragmented 
European capital market (section 2.4). All four limitations give rise to far-reaching reform proposal s of 
the oversight system in Germany and Europe. Those proposals are summarised in section 3.

Capital markets are a powerful instrument to allocate resources from investors to issuers, i.e. firms and

various contractual arrangements, regulatory or legal rules, and enforcement mechanisms, physical 
and virtual trading venues, and a variety of financial instruments, like stocks, bonds, d erivatives, and 
currencies, owned by a variety of investors. Together with the banking system, the capital market 
provides the financial infrastructure of the economy. As in banking, trust in the proper functioning of 
the capital market is a prerequisite f or it to play its beneficial role. It is, for instance, critical for broad 
investor participation (Guiso et al. 2008).

which in turn creates negative spillover effects. Scandals can make it harder for other, non-fraudulent 
firms to raise capital as investors raise the risk premium or choose to no longer participate in the market 
(e.g. Aggarwal and Wu 2006; Kyle and Viswanathan 2008; Giannetti and Wang 2016; Gurun et al. 2018).

and efficient markets, and facilitate capital formation” (SEC 2013). In a similar spirit, BaFin’s webs ite

financial market and the protection of investors.”

# Wirecard / Jan Marsalek Public Fraud Trail

## Scope and evidentiary limits

This report uses only the two benchmark sources returned by the investigation tools: the European Parliament–commissioned SAFE policy briefing and Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 announcement concerning the KPMG special audit. The SAFE briefing is an analytical policy assessment, not an official judicial finding; its authors expressly note the risk of hindsight bias and that the opinions are their own. Jan Marsalek-specific evidence was **not returned** by the benchmark tools. Accordingly, no factual conclusion about his disappearance, whereabouts, role, or culpability is made here.

## Executive assessment

The returned evidence supports a public-fraud trail with five linked components:

1. **Long-running public warning signals:** allegations about Wirecard’s accounting began appearing by 2015, followed by the 2016 Zatarra report and further Financial Times reporting.
2. **Company counter-position:** in April 2020 Wirecard publicly stated that KPMG had found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no findings requiring adjustment of its 2016–2018 accounts.
3. **Audit uncertainty:** the same Wirecard announcement acknowledged that KPMG could not obtain all data required for its heightened forensic review because relevant data were controlled by third parties. The SAFE briefing states that KPMG could not verify €1 billion in foreign bank accounts.
4. **Missing assets and collapse:** in June 2020, according to the SAFE briefing, BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard; days later Wirecard filed for bankruptcy and acknowledged that €1.9 billion in financial assets were missing.
5. **Supervisory and control failures:** the SAFE authors assessed that all five lines of defence failed in some way: Wirecard’s internal controls, supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting and audit oversight bodies, and BaFin.

The evidence therefore supports a reconstruction in which early allegations and warning signals were followed by institutional responses that did not resolve the underlying uncertainty before the company’s collapse. It does **not**, on the returned evidence, establish a complete criminal attribution chain or connect Jan Marsalek to any particular act.

---

## Chronological reconstruction

### 2015–2016: Early allegations and warning signals

The SAFE briefing states that allegations concerning accounting inconsistencies appeared from 2015, including Financial Times reporting partly based on whistleblower information concerning Wirecard’s Singapore operations. In 2016, the Zatarra report accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud. These are reported allegations and accusations, not findings independently adjudicated in the returned sources. [SRC-002]

The briefing further states that the Zatarra report was followed by significant short selling and that BaFin referred some short-selling activity to German prosecutors for alleged market abuse. [SRC-002]

### January 2019: Regulatory response to renewed reporting

After a detailed January 2019 Financial Times report, BaFin requested that FREP investigate Wirecard’s financial statements. The SAFE briefing describes the Financial Times reporting as alleging inflated sales and profit figures and says the reporting was backed by internal documents. [SRC-002]

The same source states that, when short selling intensified, BaFin prohibited increases in net short-sale positions for two months and filed criminal complaints against certain short sellers and the journalist who wrote the January report. These actions show that the regulatory response included scrutiny of market participants and the journalist, while the FREP investigation concerned Wirecard’s financial statements. [SRC-002]

### October 2019–April 2020: KPMG special audit and unresolved uncertainty

Wirecard hired KPMG in October 2019 to conduct a forensic investigation. The SAFE briefing says publication of the report was delayed until April 2020 and that KPMG was unable to verify the existence of €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. [SRC-002]

Wirecard’s own 28 April 2020 announcement presented a more favorable account. It stated that:

- KPMG had found no incriminating evidence for public allegations of balance-sheet forgery;
- no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts;
- the four reviewed areas included third-party acquiring, merchant cash advance/digital lending, India, and Singapore;
- KPMG’s heightened forensic requirements could not be fully satisfied because required data were primarily controlled by third parties;
- Wirecard had supplied more than 200 million December 2019 data records, with no deviations found between reported revenues and account balances;
- KPMG had identified documentation and organizational weaknesses; and
- the 2020 annual accounts and annual press conference were delayed pending coordination with EY. [SRC-001]

This announcement was a company statement and should not be treated as an independent verification of its assertions.

### June 2020: Criminal complaint, missing assets, and bankruptcy

The SAFE briefing states that BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020. A few days later, Wirecard filed for bankruptcy and acknowledged that €1.9 billion in financial assets were missing. [SRC-002]

This is the clearest transition in the returned evidence from unresolved public allegations and audit uncertainty to an acknowledged financial shortfall and corporate insolvency.

---

## Audit uncertainty and the apparent contradiction in public messaging

The two sources describe materially different aspects of the April 2020 audit situation:

- Wirecard said KPMG found no incriminating evidence requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. [SRC-001]
- The SAFE briefing says KPMG could not verify €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. [SRC-002]
- Wirecard itself acknowledged that not all data required for KPMG’s heightened forensic requirements could be obtained because relevant data were controlled by third parties. [SRC-001]

These statements are not necessarily logically irreconcilable. The first concerns Wirecard’s characterization of whether the audit produced evidence requiring accounting adjustments; the second concerns verification of the existence of foreign bank-account funds; and the third concerns limitations on the evidentiary material available to KPMG. Nevertheless, together they demonstrate substantial uncertainty about the evidentiary basis for Wirecard’s reported assets and accounts.

The later acknowledgment of €1.9 billion in missing financial assets sharply undermined the practical reliability of the company’s earlier public reassurance, although the returned sources do not establish precisely which statements, transactions, or individuals caused the discrepancy. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

---

## Supervisory and institutional failures

The SAFE authors assess that all five lines of defence against corporate fraud and deception failed “in one way or another”:

1. Wirecard’s internal control system;
2. Wirecard’s supervisory board;
3. external audit;
4. oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing; and
5. BaFin as market supervisor. [SRC-002]

They identify the root cause, in their assessment, as a flawed market and institutional oversight architecture. They also state that signals suggesting fraudulent behavior existed years before the eventual revelation. [SRC-002]

The source frames this as a policy analysis rather than a final legal determination. It proposes stronger information flows, stronger auditor accountability, effective internal-control systems, broader BaFin investigative and enforcement powers, and clearer supervisory accountability. [SRC-002]

The evidence thus supports an assessment of **systemic or institutional supervisory weakness**, but it does not by itself prove that every named institution or individual committed a criminal offense or professional breach.

---

## Jan Marsalek

No returned benchmark source contains usable evidence about Jan Marsalek’s:

- position or conduct in the Wirecard events;
- alleged involvement in accounting or cash movements;
- date or circumstances of disappearance;
- destination or current whereabouts;
- links to intelligence services, foreign governments, or other actors; or
- legal status.

The requested “Jan Marsalek disappearance” component therefore remains **unsubstantiated in this evidence set**. It would be improper to infer his involvement merely from his association with the case or from the timing of the company’s collapse.

---

## Findings

### Finding 1 — Were there public warning signals before Wirecard’s collapse?

**Answer:** Yes. The SAFE briefing reports accounting-inconsistency allegations from 2015, the 2016 Zatarra accusations, whistleblower-linked reporting concerning Singapore, and further Financial Times reporting in 2019. These were allegations and warning signals, not independently adjudicated findings in the returned sources.  
**Supporting entities:** Wirecard; Financial Times; Zatarra report; BaFin; FREP  
**Source references:** [SRC-002]

### Finding 2 — What did Wirecard publicly claim after the KPMG review?

**Answer:** On 28 April 2020, Wirecard stated that KPMG found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. Wirecard also acknowledged documentation and organizational weaknesses and incomplete access to data required for heightened forensic testing.  
**Supporting entities:** Wirecard; KPMG; KPMG special audit report; EY  
**Source references:** [SRC-001]

### Finding 3 — What audit uncertainty remained?

**Answer:** The SAFE briefing states that KPMG could not verify €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. Wirecard’s announcement separately acknowledged that required data were not all available because they were controlled by third parties.  
**Supporting entities:** KPMG; Wirecard; KPMG special audit report  
**Source references:** [SRC-001]; [SRC-002]

### Finding 4 — What happened in June 2020?

**Answer:** According to the SAFE briefing, BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020. Days later, Wirecard filed for bankruptcy and acknowledged €1.9 billion in missing financial assets.  
**Supporting entities:** BaFin; Wirecard; BaFin criminal complaint against Wirecard; Wirecard bankruptcy filing; date: 2020-06  
**Source references:** [SRC-002]

### Finding 5 — What supervisory failures are supported by the evidence?

**Answer:** The SAFE authors assess that all five lines of defence failed in some way, including internal controls, the supervisory board, external audit, oversight bodies, and BaFin. This is an expert assessment in a policy briefing, not a judicial finding.  
**Supporting entities:** Wirecard; BaFin; SAFE policy briefing  
**Source references:** [SRC-002]

### Finding 6 — What can be established about Jan Marsalek’s disappearance?

**Answer:** Nothing specific from the returned benchmark evidence. The available sources do not discuss his disappearance or provide evidence linking him to the missing assets or the alleged fraud.  
**Supporting entities:** Jan Marsalek  
**Source references:** None returned for this proposition; the omission is an evidence limitation.

---

## Claims

- **Claim:** Wirecard faced public allegations concerning accounting inconsistencies from 2015 onward.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-002]

- **Claim:** The 2016 Zatarra report accused Wirecard of money laundering and fraud.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-002]

- **Claim:** BaFin requested a FREP investigation after a January 2019 Financial Times report.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-002]

- **Claim:** Wirecard hired KPMG in October 2019 for a forensic investigation.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-002]

- **Claim:** Wirecard stated on 28 April 2020 that KPMG had found no incriminating evidence requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-001]

- **Claim:** The SAFE briefing states that KPMG could not verify €1 billion in foreign bank accounts.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-002]

- **Claim:** BaFin filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard in June 2020.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-002]

- **Claim:** Wirecard subsequently filed for bankruptcy and acknowledged €1.9 billion in missing financial assets.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-002]

- **Claim:** The SAFE authors assess that all five lines of defence against fraud failed in some way.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-002]

- **Claim:** The returned evidence does not establish Jan Marsalek’s role in the fraud trail or the circumstances of his disappearance.  
  **Source references:** None; this is a stated evidentiary limitation, not a factual claim about Marsalek.

---

## Contradictions and tensions

### Contradiction C-1 — Wirecard reassurance versus unresolved bank-account verification

**Description:** Wirecard stated that KPMG found no incriminating evidence requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts, while the SAFE briefing states that KPMG could not verify the existence of €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. The statements address different aspects of the review and may be technically compatible, but together they reveal a significant tension between the company’s public reassurance and the audit’s verification limitations.  
**Source references:** [SRC-001]; [SRC-002]

### Contradiction C-2 — Claimed account sufficiency versus later missing assets

**Description:** Wirecard stated that prior audit measures were sufficient to prove third-party-acquiring revenues and that supplied data showed no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. The SAFE briefing later reports that Wirecard acknowledged €1.9 billion in missing financial assets. The sources do not identify the precise accounting mechanism or responsibility behind the discrepancy, but the later acknowledgment materially conflicts with confidence in the earlier public presentation.

**Description:** The SAFE briefing reports warning signals and allegations years before the collapse, yet the matter was not resolved before the June 2020 bankruptcy. This is an institutional-performance tension identified by the authors, not proof that any particular warning was conclusively correct when first made.

This is the clearest transition in the returned evidence from unresolved public allegations and audit uncertainty to an acknowledged financial shortfall and corporate insolvency.

---

## Audit uncertainty and the apparent contradiction in public messaging

The two sources describe materially different aspects of the April 2020 audit situation:

- Wirecard said KPMG found no incriminating evidence requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. [SRC-001]
- The SAFE briefing says KPMG could not verify €1 billion in foreign bank accounts. [SRC-002]
- Wirecard itself acknowledged that not all data required for KPMG’s heightened forensic requirements could be obtained because relevant data were controlled by third parties. [SRC-001]

These statements are not necessarily logically irreconcilable. The first concerns Wirecard’s characterization of whether the audit produced evidence requiring accounting adjustments; the second concerns verification of the existence of foreign bank-account funds; and the third concerns limitations on the evidentiary material available to KPMG. Nevertheless, together they demonstrate substantial uncertainty about the evidentiary basis for Wirecard’s reported assets and accounts.

The later acknowledgment of €1.9 billion in missing financial assets sharply undermined the practical reliability of the company’s earlier public reassurance, although the returned sources do not establish precisely which statements, transactions, or individuals caused the discrepancy. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

## Supervisory and institutional failures

The SAFE authors assess that all five lines of defence against corporate fraud and deception failed “in one way or another”:

1. Wirecard’s internal control system;
2. Wirecard’s supervisory board;
3. external audit;
4. oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing; and
5. BaFin as market supervisor. [SRC-002]

They identify the root cause, in their assessment, as a flawed market and institutional oversight architecture. They also state that signals suggesting fraudulent behavior existed years before the eventual revelation. [SRC-002]

The source frames this as a policy analysis rather than a final legal determination. It proposes stronger information flows, stronger auditor accountability, effective internal-control systems, broader BaFin investigative and enforcement powers, and clearer supervisory accountability. [SRC-002]

The evidence thus supports an assessment of **systemic or institutional supervisory weakness**, but it does not by itself prove that every named institution or individual committed a criminal offense or professional breach.

## Overall conclusion

The benchmark evidence supports a documented public trail from early allegations and whistleblower-linked reporting, through regulatory and audit responses, to unresolved verification problems, a June 2020 criminal complaint, and Wirecard’s acknowledgment of €1.9 billion in missing assets before bankruptcy. The strongest supported systemic conclusion is the SAFE authors’ assessment that multiple lines of defence failed, including company controls, audit, oversight bodies, and BaFin.

The evidence does not support a complete attribution of fraud to named individuals and does not provide evidence about Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. Any claim that Marsalek controlled the missing funds, fled with knowledge of the fraud, or had intelligence-related connections would be unsupported by the returned benchmark sources.
